passage: Teacher's note, Tuesday. Elizabeth and a friend sat on opposite sides of the toy farm. Elizabeth said, "Look at the red door!" Her friend frowned: "There's no door." Elizabeth stood, walked round the table and crouched. "Oh! From here it's just a wall." She came back and turned the barn halfway so both could see the door. I asked what she noticed. "She sees the back side, I see the front." 😊 Next, I'll try a picture-drawing game from two sides. — Ms Manjula

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do after her friend said there was no door?
qa.a: She walked round the table, crouched, and saw that from there it was just a wall.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's "Oh!" suggest about what she realised?
qa.a: It suggests surprise as she understood that her friend's side of the barn really looked different from her own.

qa.q: How could Ms Manjula build on this moment?
qa.a: Her planned game of drawing the same object from two sides lets Elizabeth keep checking what others can see.

qa.q: How might the friend feel once Elizabeth turned the barn?
qa.a: She would likely feel understood rather than wrong, since now she could see the door too. 🙂

grounding: A teacher records a child discovering that her friend sees a different side of the same toy barn.

passage: Behind the cowshed in their village, Payal squatted beside the buffalo and pointed. "Saurabh Bhaiya, the calf is drinking!" From the other side, her brother called, "Which calf?" Payal giggled, then paused. The big buffalo was between them. She ran around the tail and pulled him by the hand. "You can't see it from there. The buffalo is blocking you." Saurabh grinned as the tiny calf nudged its mother's belly. "Now I see it."

qa.q: What was between Payal and her brother?
qa.a: The big buffalo was between them.

qa.q: Why do you think Payal paused after giggling?
qa.a: She seems to have realised that her brother's view was blocked, so his question was not silly after all.

qa.q: What was good about the way Payal solved the problem?
qa.a: Instead of repeating herself, she brought him to her side so he could see the calf for himself.

qa.q: What would change if the calf had been on Saurabh's side instead?
qa.a: Then he would see it and Payal might be the one asking "Which calf?", showing that each view depends on where you stand.

grounding: A village girl figures out that her brother cannot see the calf because the buffalo blocks his view.

passage: Saturday morning in a Madrid flat, Alejandro held up his picture book to Nadia, who sat facing him on the sofa. "See the dragon?" Nadia shook her head. "I only see the cover, Ale." Alejandro looked at the page, then at her. Slowly he turned the book around. "Now?" "Now I see a green dragon," she said. He tried it again with the next page, flipping it toward her each time before he read.

qa.q: Where were Alejandro and Nadia sitting?
qa.a: They sat facing each other on the sofa in a Madrid flat.

qa.q: What was Alejandro thinking when he looked at the page and then at Nadia?
qa.a: He seemed puzzled at first, then worked out that the picture faced only him, so Nadia could not see what he saw.

qa.q: How could Nadia help Alejandro practise this more?
qa.a: She could keep asking, "What can I see from here?" so he checks her side before showing things.

qa.q: What is it like for Nadia once Alejandro starts flipping each page toward her?
qa.a: She can finally join in the story instead of staring at a cover, which makes reading together fun for her.

grounding: A boy learns his sister sees only the cover of a book held facing him, and turns it so she can see.

passage: In the kindergarten room, Hemant held up his drawing of a red truck. 'Manjula Ma'am, look at my truck!' Manjula sat across the table and smiled. 'I can only see white paper, Hemant.' He frowned and peered at his picture. The truck was right there. Then he walked round to her side, stood beside her and looked. Blank paper. 'Oh!' He ran back and flipped the sheet around. 'Now you see it?'

qa.q: What had Hemant drawn?
qa.a: He had drawn a red truck.

qa.q: Why did Hemant walk around to Manjula's side of the table?
qa.a: He was confused because he could see the truck, so he wanted to find out what she was seeing from where she sat.

qa.q: What went well in how Manjula responded?
qa.a: She told him simply what she saw and let him discover the reason himself, instead of turning the page for him.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had been sitting beside Hemant?
qa.a: She would have seen the truck too, and Hemant would not have had the chance to notice that views differ.

grounding: Illustrates a child recognising that someone opposite him sees a scene differently than he does.

passage: I'm Sarita. My little sister Jaya is five. Yesterday Nani sat across the dining table while Jaya read her picture book aloud. Jaya kept the book facing herself and said, 'See the cow, Nani?' Nani said, 'I see the cover.' Jaya looked puzzled, then turned the book around. She looked at it from Nani's side, then from hers, and kept flipping it. I think something clicked, but I can't be sure what she was thinking.

qa.q: Where was Nani sitting while Jaya read?
qa.a: She was sitting across the dining table.

qa.q: What does Jaya flipping the book back and forth suggest she was thinking about?
qa.a: It suggests she was puzzled and curious, working out that Nani saw a different side of the book from her own seat.

qa.q: How could Nani help Jaya practise this idea?
qa.a: She could play simple 'what can I see?' games, like holding a toy between them and asking Jaya to guess which side Nani sees.

qa.q: How does the older sibling see Jaya's behaviour?
qa.a: The older sibling finds it interesting and thinks she learned something, but admits they cannot be sure what was in her mind.

grounding: Shows a young child beginning to grasp another person's different visual view, described by an older sibling.

passage: Monday: Keerthana, five, held up her picture book to show her brother Divyansh the tiger, but she held it facing herself. "See?" she said. He only saw the back cover. Thursday: she showed him again, stopped, and asked, "Can you see it?" When he said no, she turned the book round. The next Sunday, on a video call with Paati, she held her drawing right up to the camera. "Can you see my tiger now, Paati?"

qa.q: What picture did Keerthana want to show Divyansh?
qa.a: The tiger in her picture book.

qa.q: Why might Keerthana have been surprised when Divyansh said no on Thursday?
qa.a: She was starting to realise he couldn't see what she saw, and may have felt puzzled before turning the book round.

qa.q: How could Divyansh help Keerthana keep learning this?
qa.a: Tell her what he can actually see, like "just the back cover", so she learns to check.

qa.q: What would change for Paati if Keerthana still held drawings facing herself?
qa.a: Paati would only see the back of the paper and miss the tiger entirely.

grounding: Shows a young child learning over a week that someone opposite her sees a different view of a book or picture.

passage: The platform at the small station was packed because the train was an hour late. Eshaan, six, sat on his father's shoulders. His cousin Arohi, four, stood below, squeezed between suitcases, and kept asking, "Is it coming? Is it coming?" Eshaan could see the headlight far down the track. He looked down at her and realised she could only see legs and bags. "Arohi, it's coming! It's a blue engine. It's getting bigger!"

qa.q: What colour was the engine?
qa.a: A blue engine.

qa.q: What was Eshaan thinking when he looked down at Arohi?
qa.a: He realised she could only see legs and bags, and he seemed to feel for her and want her to share the excitement.

qa.q: What else could the adults do to help Arohi in the crowd?
qa.a: Lift her up for a moment when it is safe, or keep telling her what is happening as Eshaan did.

qa.q: What is it like for Arohi on the crowded platform?
qa.a: It is probably frustrating and a little scary to see nothing but legs while everyone waits for the train.

grounding: Shows a child realising that someone standing lower in a crowd sees a very different scene from him.

passage: In the kindergarten in Nagpur, the toy farm sat on a table between Asif and Harsha. Their teacher pointed at the plastic cow. "Asif, what can Harsha see of the cow?" Asif, five, said, "Its face." Then he frowned, got up, and walked round to Harsha's chair. "Oh. You see its tail!" He went back to his side and giggled. "I see face, Harsha sees tail."

qa.q: Which animal did the teacher point at?
qa.a: The plastic cow.

qa.q: What does Asif's frown suggest before he walked round?
qa.a: He seemed unsure and curious, sensing his first answer might be wrong.

qa.q: What did the teacher's question do well, and what might come next?
qa.a: It pushed Asif to check another view himself; next the teacher could ask him to guess before he walks round.

qa.q: How might Harsha see the moment when Asif came round to that chair?
qa.a: Harsha might find it funny and feel noticed, since Asif came to see things from that side.

grounding: Shows a young child discovering that a classmate across the table sees a different side of the same toy.

passage:
"Papa, look at my dinosaur!" Ramesh, five, held up his drawing, facing himself.
Chetan, his father, looked up from the newspaper. "I can only see the back of the paper."
"It's right here!"
"From your side. From my side it's all white."
Ramesh frowned, then walked round the table and stood next to Papa. He looked at the blank back. "Oh!" He ran back and turned the paper round. "Now?"
"Now I see a big green dinosaur with… is that a crown?"
"He's a king dinosaur."
"Of course he is."

qa.q: What colour was the dinosaur?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's frown suggest?
qa.a: Ramesh felt puzzled and confused that Papa couldn't see the drawing.

qa.q: How did Chetan help Ramesh understand another person's view?
qa.a: He described what he saw from his side and let Ramesh walk round to see the blank back himself.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel when Ramesh turns the paper round?
qa.a: Chetan probably feels amused and pleased, seeing his son work it out.

grounding: A father helps his five-year-old discover that someone on the other side sees a different view of a drawing.

passage: Kindergarten note, December. While we decorated the class Christmas tree, Sangeeta (5) stood at the front and told Meenu, "Put the bell next to the red ball!" Meenu, on the other side of the tree, couldn't see any red ball and got upset. I asked Sangeeta, "Can Meenu see what you see?" She walked round to Meenu's side, looked, and said, "Oh, the ball is hiding from you." Then she said, "Put it near the star," which both of them could see. I'll try a "what can your friend see" game at circle time. — Jaya Ma'am

qa.q: Where was Meenu standing?
qa.a: On the other side of the tree.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she saw the tree from Meenu's side?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt surprised to find the red ball hidden from Meenu's side.

qa.q: What will Jaya Ma'am try next, and why?
qa.a: A 'what can your friend see' game at circle time, to practise noticing that others see things differently.

qa.q: How might Meenu have felt before Sangeeta changed her instruction?
qa.a: Meenu was probably confused and upset, unable to find the red ball.

grounding: A teacher's Christmas-season note shows a five-year-old realising a friend sees the tree differently.

passage: At harvest time in their village near Nanded, Samir, five, sat high on the tractor seat beside his Abba. "Payal! Look at the calf!" he shouted to his little cousin on the ground. "Where?" Payal, four, spun round. "There! Behind the sugarcane!" Payal jumped, but saw only green stalks. Samir looked down at her, then at the tall cane. "Oh. You're too small." He climbed down, took her hand, and walked her round the edge of the field until they found the calf.

qa.q: Where was the calf?
qa.a: Behind the sugarcane.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when he looked down at Payal?
qa.a: Samir felt surprised, realising Payal was too small to see over the cane from the ground.

qa.q: How did Samir solve the problem once he understood Payal's view?
qa.a: He climbed down, took her hand, and walked her round the field to where she could see the calf.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt jumping but seeing only stalks?
qa.a: Payal probably felt frustrated and left out, unable to see what Samir was excited about.

grounding: At harvest time, a village five-year-old realises his small cousin cannot see what he sees from the tractor.

passage:
At the Chinese New Year party at their kindergarten in Singapore, Nkechi and Mei sat on opposite sides of a big paper lion head.

"Look at its big eyes!" Nkechi said.

"I can't see eyes," said Mei. "I can see the tail."

Nkechi frowned. She could see the eyes clearly. She stood up, walked around to Mei's side, and looked.

"Oh! From here it's all tail," she said. "Come to my side and see the eyes."

qa.q: What could Mei see from her side?
qa.a: Mei could see the tail.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel when Mei said she couldn't see the eyes?
qa.a: Nkechi felt puzzled, frowning, because she could see the eyes clearly herself.

qa.q: How could a teacher build on Nkechi's discovery?
qa.a: Ask the children to sit in different spots and describe what they see, then swap places to check.

qa.q: How might Mei feel when Nkechi invited her to swap sides?
qa.a: Mei would likely feel happy and included, getting to see the eyes too.

grounding: At a Chinese New Year party, a child realises a friend sitting on the other side sees a different part of the same object.

passage:
The nursery school hall was decorated for Christmas, with a crib scene on a low table. Pankaj sat on one side and Sahil on the other.

"Look at the baby!" Pankaj said.

"Where? I only see a donkey," Sahil said.

Pankaj thought for a moment. Then he said, "Oh, the donkey is in front on your side. The baby is on my side." He came and stood beside Sahil. "See? You can't see the baby from here."

qa.q: What could Sahil see from his side?
qa.a: Sahil only saw a donkey.

qa.q: What was Pankaj thinking when he said the donkey was in front on Sahil's side?
qa.a: Pankaj was curious and working it out, realising that Sahil's view was different from his own.

qa.q: How can the teacher encourage this kind of thinking?
qa.a: Ask children to describe what they see from different seats and then swap places to check.

qa.q: What was it like for Sahil when Pankaj came to stand beside him?
qa.a: Sahil likely felt understood and pleased when Pankaj saw that he really couldn't see the baby.

grounding: In a nursery school at Christmas, a child realises that his friend sees the crib scene differently from the other side.

passage:
I'm Pooja, Mridul's mother. On Diwali morning, he and I made a rangoli peacock on the doorstep. I was kneeling on the outside, and he was on the inside.

"Can you see the peacock's crown, Mumma?" he asked.

"It looks upside down from here," I said.

He frowned. Then he got up, came round to my side, and looked. "It is upside down for you!" He giggled and drew a second crown facing me.

qa.q: What did Mridul draw facing Pooja?
qa.a: He drew a second crown facing her.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel when he saw the peacock was upside down from Pooja's side?
qa.a: Mridul seemed surprised and amused, giggling when he found it was upside down for her.

qa.q: How can Pooja keep encouraging Mridul to think about other views?
qa.a: Keep asking what he thinks she sees from where she is, and let him check by walking around.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when Mridul drew a crown facing her?
qa.a: Pooja was likely touched and delighted that he thought of her view.

grounding: A mother observes her son realising that a rangoli looks different from her side and adapting it for her.

passage:
Monday before Diwali: Sharmila held up her picture book, pages facing herself, and asked Deepak across the table, "See the elephant?" Deepak said, "I see the cover!"
Diwali morning: They drew a rangoli peacock on the doorstep. From the other side, Deepak said, "It's upside down." Sharmila walked round to where he stood, stared, and giggled. "It is, from there!"
Two days later: Showing Nani her drawing, Sharmila turned the page round first so it faced Nani.

qa.q: What did the children draw on the doorstep on Diwali morning?
qa.a: They drew a rangoli peacock on the doorstep.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's giggle on Diwali morning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was surprised and amused to find the peacock really did look upside down from Deepak's side.

qa.q: How could Nani help Sharmila keep practising this?
qa.a: She could play games like "What can you see from my chair?" and let Sharmila walk round to check.

qa.q: How does Deepak experience the picture book on Monday?
qa.a: Deepak can only see the cover, so Sharmila's question makes no sense from his seat and he is a little puzzled.

grounding: Illustrates a young child learning, over a festival week, that someone across the way sees a picture differently.
